title: Living for someone else
hookLine: Seneca cares for his health for his wife Paulina's sake (Letters 104)

cards: Here's a small scene from a marriage. One of you is getting sick, and wants to push through. The other says: please, just go and rest.

And you go, not because you're convinced, but because you can see the worry on their face. In the hundred-and-fourth letter, Seneca feels a fever coming on in Rome, and leaves for his farm at Nomentum, outside the city.
His wife Paulina, he says, keeps urging him to look after his health. On the way, he thinks about what we owe our own bodies when someone else depends on us.

teach.b: First, Paulina. Seneca says she kept urging him to look after his health. And because he knows, he writes, that her life is bound up with his, he has begun to take care of himself in order to take care of her.
Old age had made him bolder about many things, he admits, and careless about his body. For her sake, he lets that go. Second, the indulgence.
He calls this an honest indulgence, a soft spot he isn't ashamed of.

Some people think the wise should be indifferent to their own health. Seneca says no: a good person will sometimes hold on to life, and look after it, for the sake of those they love, even when they'd personally shrug.
Third, the larger point. Caring for yourself isn't always selfish. Sometimes it's a gift.
A parent who sees a doctor, a friend who finally sleeps, a partner who takes the medicine: they're doing it for someone. Fourth, the history.
Tacitus, the Roman historian, tells us Paulina outlived Seneca by a few years, and kept an honored memory of her husband.

teach.h: PAULINA'S NAME, STILL IN THE LETTER.
teach.b: Her name is still attached to this kindness in a letter.
Tomorrow, the same letter turns to Socrates.

how: Readers of this letter often think of looking after their own health as something they do for the people who depend on them, not only for themselves.

o: a little treat you allow yourself when sad
forgiving a friend more easily than you should
caring for your health for a loved one's sake

p: says she outlived him by a few years

s: Seneca says a wise person should ignore their health entirely
he says a good person sometimes cares for life for the sake of loved ones.
Seneca looked after himself because Paulina's life was bound up with his
he took care of himself in order to take care of her.
Seneca is ashamed of caring for himself for Paulina's sake
he calls it an honest indulgence, nothing to be ashamed of.

games.q: you're old, a fever is starting, and you'd shrug it off. your partner is worried sick. what does Seneca do?
o: ignore it: a wise man doesn't care.
take care of himself, for her sake.
games.why: Seneca says knowing her life depends on his, he began caring for himself in order to care for her.

practice: Think of one person who'd be affected if you didn't look after yourself, a partner, a child, a friend, even a pet who waits by the door, and picture their face.
Then think of one small care you've let slide, sleep, a checkup, a walk, and imagine doing it for their sake, as a gift rather than a chore.

wordCard.voice: Honesta indulgentia. Seneca's phrase for caring for his own health, for his wife Paulina's sake, and calling it an honest indulgence he isn't ashamed of. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: an honorable indulgence, Seneca's phrase in Letters 104.4 for caring for himself for Paulina's sake.

carryVoice: Your line: for paulina. Looking after yourself can be a kindness to someone else. That's day four hundred eighty-one.
